section_1a.directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements below is followed by four suggested answers or completions. Select the one that is best in each case. You have 55 minutes.

questions.stimulus: Annual growth of output per person (percent), by region — 1700–1820: World 0.1, Europe 0.1, Americas 0.4, Africa 0.0, Asia 0.0; 1820–1913: World 0.9, Europe 1.0, Americas 1.5, Africa 0.04, Asia 0.02; 1913–1950: World 0.9, Europe 0.9, Americas 1.4, Africa 0.9, Asia 0.2; 1950–1970: World 2.8, Europe 3.8, Americas 1.9, Africa 2.1, Asia 3.5; 1970–1990: World 1.3, Europe 1.9, Americas 1.6, Africa 0.3, Asia 2.1; 1990–2012: World 2.1, Europe 1.9, Americas 1.5, Africa 1.4, Asia 3.4. —Data adapted from Thomas Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century, 2013
questions.stem: The Americas' strong per-person growth between 1820 and 1913 was driven above all by
options: (A) The independence movements that freed Latin America from Spain and Portugal.
(B) The California gold rush of 1849.
(C) European immigration to Argentina and southern Brazil.
(D) Rapid industrialization in the United States.

questions.stimulus:
In 1804, the Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio proclaimed a jihad in what is now northern Nigeria, denouncing the Hausa kings for corruption, unjust taxation, and un-Islamic practices. His followers overthrew the Hausa states and founded the Sokoto Caliphate.

The accusation was specific: the Hausa kings levied taxes Islam did not sanction, mixed Islamic observance with local custom, and — in dan Fodio's telling — oppressed Muslim scholars and commoners alike. The jihad was thus framed as reform, not conquest: a return to proper Islam against rulers who were Muslim in name only. It was fellow Muslims, not outsiders, who were the primary target.
questions.stem: The jihad proclaimed in the passage was directed mainly against
options: (A) Buddhist kingdoms
(B) Hausa rulers accused of corruption
(C) European colonizers of the later 1800s
(D) the Ottoman Empire

questions.stimulus: From a letter by Lin Zexu, Chinese imperial commissioner, to Queen Victoria (1839): Lin protested that Britain was sending China a 'poisonous drug' — opium — out of an 'inordinate thirst after gain,' careless of the harm done. He noted that opium was strictly prohibited in Britain itself, 'a strong proof that you know full well how hurtful it is to mankind,' and asked why Britain would send to China what it banned at home.
questions.stem: Lin's letter was written on the eve of which conflict?
options: (A) The Boxer Rebellion
(B) The Taiping Rebellion
(C) The First Opium War between Britain and China
(D) The Sino-Japanese War

questions.stimulus: Text excerpt: strategies rulers used to legitimize power, c. 1450-1750. Ottoman sultans: claimed the title of caliph as protectors of Sunni Islam and built great mosques. Safavid shahs: claimed connection to the Shi'a Imams and devotion to Twelver Shi'ism. Mughal emperors under Akbar: presented the emperor as a divine light above sectarian division. Qing emperors: claimed the Mandate of Heaven and patronized Confucian rites. Tokugawa shoguns: upheld the Neo-Confucian social hierarchy as the natural order. Russian tsars: claimed Moscow as the Third Rome, heir to Orthodox Byzantium.
questions.stem: Which of the following arguments about early modern legitimation is best supported by the table?
options: (A) Every empire in the period used exactly the same religious justification, sacred language, public rituals, and clerical hierarchy to legitimize its rule.
(B) Rulers tailored divine sanction to local traditions — Shi'a Islam in Persia, Sunni Islam in Ottoman lands, Confucian cosmology in China.
(C) Religious legitimation was unimportant, since all of these rulers relied on military force alone.
(D) Protestant Christianity was the dominant legitimating faith across Eurasia in this period.

questions.stimulus: A Jewish merchant in medieval India wrote home to his wife: 'Now if divorce is your wish, I cannot blame you. For the waiting has been long... I cannot come home with nothing.' He had been stranded abroad for months, unable to sail until the winds turned.
questions.stem: The long absences described were structured by which of the following?
options: (A) The Mongol invasions of the Middle East
(B) The monsoon wind cycle
(C) The weekly observance of the Jewish Sabbath
(D) The military campaigns of the Crusades

questions.stimulus: As sugar plantations spread across Brazil and the Caribbean, European traders purchased millions of captive Africans. African states and merchants took part in supplying captives through wars and raids, and the Middle Passage across the Atlantic killed roughly one in seven of those forced aboard.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is best supported by the passage?
options: (A) The transatlantic slave trade was driven by plantation labor demand and operated through European demand, African political participation, and immense human mortality.
(B) The slave trade was economically insignificant to the development of the Atlantic economy.
(C) Europeans captured all enslaved Africans directly themselves, marching far inland to seize captives with absolutely no participation by any African states or merchants.
(D) Slavery in the Americas ended everywhere when the slave trade was abolished in 1807.

questions.stimulus:
Source 1: I want to say to you who think women cannot succeed, we have brought the government of England to this position, that it has to face this alternative; either women are to be killed or women are to have the vote. I ask American men in this meeting, what would you say if in your State you were faced with that alternative? Well, there is only one answer to that alternative; you must give those women the vote. Now that is the outcome of our civil war.

Source: 'Militant Suffragist,' Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913

Source 2: A woman whose husband owns a sugar mill or hacienda and calls herself a Spiritist or Christian should not seek to load herself down with jewelry, nor make useless purchases. She should visit the families of her peons, who produce the wealth she and her husband possess, and observe how they live, if they lack chairs, beds, and other utensils. And if you find opposition from your husband, if he is cruel and egotistical and becomes an obstacle to your great and just aspirations, do not blame him and do not fear him; because in him, you will see the symbol of ignorance, trying to hold on to its power. Oh woman! You will set a great and dignified example by breaking traditional customs, which are unjust and tyrannical, in order to establish the realm of Freedom, Equality, and Fraternity!

Source: 'Mi Opinion,' Luisa Capetillo, 1911
questions.stem: Pankhurst's description of the suffrage struggle as 'our civil war' most clearly reflects which of the following about her movement's tactics?
options: (A) Pankhurst advocated the violent overthrow of the British government.
(B) The WSPU relied solely on peaceful petitioning and gradual persuasion.
(C) Pankhurst opposed any cooperation with American suffragists.
(D) The British suffragettes used militant, confrontational tactics to force political concessions.

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of the Qianlong emperor's 1793 reply to King George III's embassy seeking expanded trade: Strange and costly objects do not interest me. Your tribute offerings are accepted only in recognition of the loyal spirit that sent them from afar. As your ambassador has seen, we possess all things; I set no value on curious or ingenious objects and have no use for your country's manufactures. Show still greater devotion and loyalty hereafter, so that by perpetual submission to our throne you may secure peace and prosperity.
questions.stem: China accepted mainly silver in payment for its tea, silk, and porcelain. What was the global effect of this policy?
options: (A) Silver became worthless worldwide
(B) China refused to accept silver
(C) Europe stopped mining silver entirely, relying on recycled coinage for its currency
(D) The world's silver streamed to China, financing Spanish America's mining boom

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of an account given to a French officer in Algeria in the 1830s by a member of an Arab slave-trading caravan: The soldiers are summoned to hunt the 'Koholanes,' a pejorative term for black Africans. They split into companies with orders to attack undefended villages and seize peasants working their fields. While awaiting the raiders' return, the narrator visits the slave market daily, recording prices in cowries: a bearded adult man, 10-15,000 (considered poor merchandise, likely to escape); an adult woman, 10-15,000 for the same reason; an adolescent boy, 30,000; a young woman, 50-60,000 depending on beauty; a boy child, 45,000; a girl child, 35-40,000. The caravan, which left Algeria with sixty-four camels and sixteen men, now numbers four hundred captives, three hundred of them women. At one point the captives erupt in cries and sobs; some throw themselves down, cling to bushes, and refuse to walk until driven on by bloody lashings.
questions.stem: Islamic law forbade enslaving fellow Muslims. How did the raiders' summons to hunt the 'idolatrous Koholanes' function?
options: (A) The raiders were Christians
(B) The label was meaningless rhetoric
(C) Islamic law forbade Muslims from owning any slaves, requiring all captives to be freed
(D) Labeling captives as idolaters made their enslavement religiously permissible

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Rudyard Kipling's 'Gunga Din' (1890): The narrator, a British soldier in India, recalls the regiment's bhisti, or water carrier, Gunga Din, a man the soldiers mocked and beat. With only a rag and a goatskin water bag for equipment, Din followed the regiment through every battle, fearless under fire. One night the narrator, wounded and choking with thirst, was found by Din, who gave him foul water, staunched his wound, and carried him to safety, taking a bullet himself. Dying, Din asked only if the narrator liked his drink. The soldier closes: though I beat and cursed you, you are a better man than I am, Gunga Din.
questions.stem: The narrator closes by admitting he once 'beat and cursed' Gunga Din. What does this admission change about the final tribute?
options: (A) The praise becomes a confession of guilt: the narrator honors a man he himself abused
(B) The narrator reveals he never actually met Gunga Din
(C) The admission proves the narrator promoted Din to officer rank
(D) The poem is really a boast about the narrator's own battlefield heroism

questions.stimulus:
Source 1: 'We, men and women, who hereby constitute ourselves as the National Organization for Women, believe that the time has come for a new movement toward true equality for all women in America, and toward a fully equal partnership of the sexes, as part of the world-wide revolution of human rights now taking place within and beyond our national borders. The purpose of NOW is to take action to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now, exercising all the privileges and responsibilities thereof in truly equal partnership with men.'

Source: National Organization for Women, Statement of Purpose, 1966

Source 2: 'The long-term goal of Gay Liberation is to rid society of the gender-role system which is at the root of our oppression. This can only be achieved by eliminating the social pressures on men and women to conform to narrowly defined gender roles. As the abolition of gender roles is also a necessary condition of women's liberation, we will work to form a strategic alliance with the women's liberation movement. In order to build this alliance, the brothers in gay liberation will have to be prepared to sacrifice that degree of male chauvinism and male privilege that they still all possess.'

Source: Gay Liberation Front, Manifesto, 1971
questions.stem: The manifesto's demand that gay men sacrifice their 'male chauvinism and male privilege' best illustrates which of the following?
options: (A) The manifesto blames women for the oppression of gay people.
(B) The GLF saw no connection between sexism and the oppression of gay people.
(C) The GLF rejected any alliance with the feminist movement.
(D) The movement said gay men could perpetuate sexism and had to confront it.

questions.stimulus: Annual growth of output per person (percent), by region — 1700–1820: World 0.1, Europe 0.1, Americas 0.4, Africa 0.0, Asia 0.0; 1820–1913: World 0.9, Europe 1.0, Americas 1.5, Africa 0.04, Asia 0.02; 1913–1950: World 0.9, Europe 0.9, Americas 1.4, Africa 0.9, Asia 0.2; 1950–1970: World 2.8, Europe 3.8, Americas 1.9, Africa 2.1, Asia 3.5; 1970–1990: World 1.3, Europe 1.9, Americas 1.6, Africa 0.3, Asia 2.1; 1990–2012: World 2.1, Europe 1.9, Americas 1.5, Africa 1.4, Asia 3.4. —Data adapted from Thomas Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century, 2013
questions.stem: A student claims the table shows which regions produced the most total goods in each period. What is the flaw in this reading?
options: (A) The figures show the growth of each region's population over time, not its economic output.
(B) The figures show government spending, not private production.
(C) The figures show growth in each person's share of output, not total output.
(D) The figures show trade balances between the regions.

questions.stimulus:
The new Imperialism has nowhere extended the political and civil liberties of the mother country to any part of the vast territories which, since 1870, have fallen under the government of Western civilized Powers. Politically, the new Imperialism is an expansion of autocracy.

Taking the growth of Imperialism as illustrated in the recent expansion of Great Britain and of the chief continental Powers, we find the distinction between Imperialism and colonization closely borne out by facts and figures, and warranting the following general judgments: First, almost the whole of recent imperial expansion is occupied with the political absorption of tropical or sub-tropical lands in which white men will not settle with their families. Second, nearly all the lands are thickly peopled by 'lower races.'

Thus this recent imperial expansion stands entirely distinct from the colonisation of sparsely peopled lands in temperate zones, where white colonists carry with them the modes of government, the industrial and other arts of the civilisation of the mother country. The 'occupation' of these new territories is comprised in the presence of a small minority of white men, officials, traders, and industrial organisers, exercising political and economic sway over great hordes of population regarded as inferior and as incapable of exercising any considerable rights of self-government, in politics or industry.

Source: Imperialism, A Study by English economist John A. Hobson (1902)
questions.stem: Hobson's reference to colonized peoples as 'lower races' is most significant as evidence that
options: (A) Hobson rejected the racial hierarchies accepted by most Europeans of his time.
(B) Hobson supported the continued expansion of the British Empire.
(C) Even a critic of imperialism in 1902 shared the racial assumptions of his era.
(D) Hobson's critique of imperialism was grounded in Marxist revolutionary theory.

questions.stimulus: In recent years the spontaneous forces of capitalism have steadily grown in our countryside: new rich peasants spring up everywhere, and many well-to-do middle peasants strive to become rich peasants. Meanwhile many poor peasants still live in poverty for lack of sufficient means of production, some in debt and others selling or renting out their land. If this tendency goes unchecked, the polarization of the countryside will inevitably grow worse day by day. The peasants who lose their land and those who remain in poverty will complain that we do nothing to save them from ruin; nor will the well-to-do middle peasants heading down the capitalist road be pleased with us, for we can never satisfy their demands unless we take the capitalist road ourselves. Can the worker-peasant alliance continue to stand in these circumstances? Obviously not. There is no solution except on a new basis: to bring about, step by step, the socialist transformation of the whole of agriculture, together with socialist industrialization and the socialist transformation of handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce — in other words, to carry out cooperation and eliminate the rich-peasant economy and the individual economy in the countryside, so that all rural people grow well-off together. This alone will consolidate the worker-peasant alliance. — Mao Zedong, On the Question of Agricultural Cooperation, 1955
questions.stem: Mao's drive for rapid agricultural collectivization, urged in this speech, culminated in which of the following?
options: (A) The immediate adoption of capitalist family farming nationwide.
(B) China's withdrawal from the United Nations.
(C) The Great Leap Forward and its devastating famine.
(D) A verified doubling of grain output by 1960.

questions.stimulus: The photograph, dated September 1939, shows German infantry and armored vehicles advancing across the Polish frontier as Polish border posts burn in the background.
questions.stem: The photograph shows German troops and tanks crossing into Poland in September 1939. What did this invasion most directly cause?
options: (A) Britain and France declared war on Germany
(B) The Soviet Union immediately joined Britain and France
(C) The United States immediately entered the war
(D) German forces were stopped at the Polish border

questions.stimulus:
Since the Sung dynasty had lost the throne and Heaven had cut off their sacrifice, the Yuan dynasty had risen from the desert to enter and rule over China for more than a hundred years, when Heaven, wearied of their misgovernment and debauchery, thought also fit to turn their fate to ruin, and the affairs of China were in a state of disorder for eighteen years. But when the nation began to arouse itself, We conceived the patriotic idea to save the people, and it pleased the Creator to grant that Our civil and military officers effected their passage across the River. We have then been engaged in war for fourteen years; We have established peace in the Empire, and restored the old boundaries of China. We were selected by Our people to occupy the Imperial throne under the dynastic title of 'the Great Ming.' We now send a native of your country to hand you this Manifesto. Although We are not equal in wisdom to our ancient rulers, We cannot but let the world know Our intention to maintain peace within the four seas.

Source: Manifesto of Accession as First Ming Emperor, 1372 (sent to the Byzantine emperor)
questions.stem: The manifesto's explanation for the fall of the Yuan dynasty relies most heavily on which of the following ideas?
options: (A) The author claims the Ming won because of superior military technology alone.
(B) The manifesto argues the Yuan fell because they abandoned Buddhist practices.
(C) The author presents the Ming as a continuation of Mongol rule in China.
(D) The author legitimizes the Ming by claiming Heaven withdrew its favor from the misruled Yuan.

questions.stimulus: Two images: a portrait of Leonard Parkinson, a Maroon resistance fighter in Jamaica (c. 1796), and a map showing Cossack hosts scattered along the frontiers of the former Russian Empire. Maroons were communities of escaped enslaved people; Cossacks were frontier horsemen on the steppe borderlands.
questions.stem: Societies like those shown were able to form mainly because
options: (A) they possessed industrial-era weapons
(B) Central states could not reach frontier zones
(C) European empires actively encouraged their formation
(D) they received massive foreign military aid

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Martin Luther's 1520 Address to the Christian Nobility of the German Nation: Luther lays before Germany's princes a program for reforming the Christian estate, driven, he says, not by arrogance but by the distress oppressing all Christendom, especially Germany. Rome, he charges, has built three walls around itself so that no one can reform it, and Christendom has suffered terribly behind them: first, the claim that temporal rulers have no authority over spiritual matters; second, that no one but the pope may interpret the scriptures; third, that no one but the pope may call a council. He then turns to what a true council should address, above all the worldly extravagance of the papacy. It is, he writes, a dreadful thing to see the man who calls himself Christ's vicar living in pomp no king or emperor can match. As for the cardinals, their real function is plain: Italy and Germany hold rich convents, endowments, and benefices, and Rome created cardinals and handed them these prizes as the surest way to drag the wealth into Roman hands, destroying genuine service to God in the process.
questions.stem: Beyond doctrine, the Council of Trent ordered bishops to reside in their dioceses and created seminaries to train priests. What problem did these disciplinary reforms address?
options: (A) Overpopulation in the Papal States and the Italian peninsula
(B) A decline in religious art
(C) Absenteeism, corruption, and ignorance among the clergy
(D) Excessive education among priests

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Baldassare Castiglione's The Courtier (1528): The ideal court lady should be learned in letters, music, and painting, graceful in dance and conversation, witty and pleasant, and adorned with virtue, continence, and prudence. Castiglione notes that even Plato, no great friend to women, entrusted them with guarding the city. He distinguishes the court lady from a queen only in that he does not lay martial duties upon her. History, he adds, records women who waged wars and won victories, governed kingdoms with prudence and justice, excelled in philosophy and poetry, and pleaded cases eloquently before judges.
questions.stem: Castiglione invokes Plato to defend women's capacities. How does this show Renaissance humanism at work?
options: (A) He rejected classical antiquity as pagan error, irrelevant to any modern question
(B) Plato opposed educating women
(C) He used classical authority to support new ideas about human potential
(D) Humanists ignored the classics

questions.stimulus:
My lord, you may have seen by the maps of Asia how great every way is the extent of the empire of the Great Mogul, which is commonly called India. In this country there are sundry nations which the Mogul is not full master of, most of them still retaining their particular sovereigns and lords that neither obey him nor pay him tribute but from constraint; many that do little, some that do nothing at all, and some also that receive tribute from him.

Such are the Pathans, a Mohammedan people toward Bengal, who before the invasion of the Moguls in India had made themselves potent in many places, and chiefly at Delhi, and had rendered many rajahs thereabout their tributaries. These Pathans are fierce and warlike, and even the meanest of them, though they be but waiting men and porters, are still of a very high spirit.

Source: An Account of India and the Great Moghul, by Francois Bernier, 1655
questions.stem: Bernier's description of the peoples within the Mughal Empire best supports which of the following conclusions about Mughal rule?
options: (A) The Mughals ruled through a uniform and fully centralized imperial bureaucracy.
(B) The Pathans were the Mughal emperors' most loyal and obedient frontier subjects.
(C) Mughal authority was layered and negotiated, with many groups keeping autonomy.
(D) Bernier's account proves the Mughal Empire was already in decline by 1655.

questions.stimulus:
'To the Merchants, Clothiers and all such as wish well to the Staple Manufactory of this Nation. The humble address and petition of thousands, who labour in the Cloth Manufactory, sheweth that the scribbling-machines have thrown thousands of your petitioners out of employ, whereby they are brought into great distress. The number of scribbling-machines extending about seventeen miles south-west of Leeds exceed all belief, being no less than one hundred and seventy! And as each machine will do as much work in twelve hours as ten men can in that time do by hand, and they working night and day, one machine will do as much work in one day as would otherwise employ twenty men.'

Source: 1786 petition by the Leeds (England) woolen workers
questions.stem: The petition's deferential tone and appeal to lay aside 'prejudice and self-interest' best illustrate which of the following about the petitioners' strategy?
options: (A) They threaten violent revolution if the machines are not removed at once.
(B) They appeal to the merchants' reason and conscience rather than force.
(C) They demand the right to vote for Parliament.
(D) They appeal directly to the king for protection.

questions.stimulus: A French philosopher writing in 1949 argued that throughout history, women's near-constant cycles of pregnancy, childbirth, and nursing absorbed their strength and time, leaving them dependent on men for protection and food. Meanwhile, she wrote, men used tools to turn survival into an active project, while motherhood kept women 'riveted to her body.' She insisted this difference was not natural destiny but a material condition that shaped women's unequal social position. (Paraphrased from Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, 1949.)
questions.stem: A historian could most productively use this passage as evidence for which claim?
options: (A) Postwar feminists reframed women's inequality as a product of social and material conditions
(B) French feminists writing in 1949 completely rejected every single idea ever associated with Marxism
(C) De Beauvoir considered voting rights unimportant for women's freedom
(D) Reliable contraception was already universally available by 1949

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of a Japanese WWII English-language radio broadcast to American troops: Hello, Yankee brothers. This is your Japanese sister, the Voice of Truth. This morning your superiors are sending you to attempt the impossible, for you cannot dislodge our forces. I am filled with sadness for you, thinking of the thousands of Japanese soldiers safe in caves and pillboxes your bombs cannot touch, reluctantly waiting to slaughter you. They bear you no ill will; they know what you attempt is futile. Why die for people who sit snug and secure 11,000 miles away?
questions.stem: The broadcast addresses American GIs as 'Yankee brothers,' pities them, and insists Japanese defenses are invulnerable. What was the strategic purpose?
options: (A) To sap American soldiers' will to fight by making battle seem hopeless
(B) To provide accurate war news
(C) To recruit Japanese soldiers
(D) To praise American commanders

questions.stimulus: A modern historian summarizes Japan's transformation: after decades of weakness, it was good to be Japanese at last, and to humble the mighty neighbor that had dominated the horizon for so long. In under forty years, Japan had gone from a feudal society to a modern state — with advanced weaponry, a professional military bureaucracy, reformed governing structures, and a new educational system reaching the whole population.
questions.stem: The Meiji slogan 'rich country, strong army' (fukoku kyohei) best reflects which priority of the new government?
options: (A) Industrial and military strength to resist the West
(B) Restoring the shogun's traditional authority
(C) Making Japan fully self-sufficient in raw materials
(D) Spreading democratic government throughout Japan

questions.stimulus: [Image 1: A 1577 woodcut of an Ottoman janissary — a mustached infantryman in a tall cap, carrying a long musket over his shoulder and holding a burning match cord. Image 2: A Japanese painting from the late 1500s showing two soldiers in robes aiming long matchlock muskets.]
questions.stem: The janissary's musket and match cord reflect the Ottomans' practice of
options: (A) Relying on heavily armored knights fighting on horseback in the medieval European fashion.
(B) Refusing to adopt any gunpowder weapons at all.
(C) Fielding a professional standing infantry equipped with the newest firearms.
(D) Hiring only short-term tribal levies for each campaign.

questions.stimulus: A map shows the major Cossack hosts of the former Russian Empire — the Don, Kuban, Terek, Ural, Siberian, and others — scattered along the empire's southern and eastern frontiers, each labeled with its host name and general territory.
questions.stem: Which of the following important aspects of Cossack history can NOT be learned from the map alone?
options: (A) The general location of the Cossack hosts
(B) That the hosts were spread across frontier regions
(C) The names of the major hosts
(D) The great Cossack revolts, like Pugachev's

questions.stimulus:
A historian argues that China's rulers invested less in early gunpowder artillery not from cultural blindness but because their most dangerous enemies were mobile nomadic horsemen of the northern steppe — against whom heavy, slow-firing cannon were nearly useless.

The transmission routes ran both ways across Eurasia: gunpowder recipes and casting techniques traveled west with the Mongol conquests, while improved European cannon designs later flowed back east. What the Islamic world did not import wholesale was the institutional package — standing, drilled infantry armies — that eventually made gunpowder decisive in Europe.
questions.stem: According to historians who defend the rationality of China's choices, Ming military investment focused instead on
options: (A) Defending the northern frontier against nomads
(B) Building a blue-water navy to conquer Europe outright
(C) Developing nuclear weapons
(D) Abandoning all military spending

questions.stimulus: The Louisiana Purchase, 1803: France sold the Louisiana Territory — stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains — to the United States for $15 million, doubling the country's size. Background: French forces in Saint-Domingue (Haiti) were defeated by revolution and disease, 1801–1803; Haitian independence followed in 1804.
questions.stem: This account best supports which causal explanation for the Louisiana Purchase?
options: (A) Defeat in Saint-Domingue convinced Napoleon to abandon his American empire project and sell Louisiana to the United States
(B) Napoleon sold Louisiana in order to raise money to fund and arm the Haitian rebels and their navy in their fight against the British
(C) The United States conquered Louisiana by force from France
(D) France retained Louisiana and never actually sold the territory

questions.stimulus:
During the Crusades, Muslim and Christian rulers preached holy war against each other — yet in the ports and markets of the Levant, Muslim, Christian, and Jewish merchants continued to trade, lend, and even partner with one another throughout the fighting.

The explanation lies in the separation of spheres. Holy war was the business of rulers and clerics, proclaimed in sermons and legal opinions; trade was the business of merchants, governed by contracts, partnerships, and the practical need for goods. Italian city-states signed commercial treaties with Muslim rulers even as popes preached crusades, and the customs houses of Alexandria collected their duties through every war. Ideology set the rhetoric; interest kept the ships sailing.
questions.stem: The coexistence of holy-war rhetoric with ongoing commerce is best explained by
options: (A) Practical needs of trade overriding official hostilities
(B) the absence of any real religious differences between the faiths
(C) decisive European military victories
(D) the complete end of all warfare

questions.stimulus: France's colonial doctrine of 'assimilation' held that colonial subjects could become French by adopting French language, culture, and values — measuring civilization by Frenchness. The negritude writers, educated in that very system, answered it with poetry affirming the worth of African cultures on their own terms.
questions.stem: Negritude differed from the French colonial ideal of 'assimilation' in that it
options: (A) Supported the continuation of French colonialism
(B) rejected the use of the French language
(C) Valued African cultures on their own terms
(D) demanded that all Africans move to France

questions.stimulus: Aerial color photograph, Keppel Container Terminal, Singapore, 2012: towering gantry cranes loom over acres of stacked multicolored steel shipping containers, with large container ships docked at the quays and dozens more vessels anchored offshore.
questions.stem: Which of the following is the best-supported argument about the development shown in the photograph?
options: (A) container shipping ended all government regulation of international trade
(B) falling transport costs let firms split production across countries, accelerating export-led industrialization in East and Southeast Asia
(C) containerization mainly benefited wealthy countries and had little effect on developing economies
(D) standardized containers made multinational corporations unnecessary

questions.stimulus: "If I were to record the services I have rendered the French government, I should need many volumes. As a reward, I have been arbitrarily arrested at St. Domingo, bound, and put on board ship like a criminal, without regard for my rank. I was once worth 648,000 francs; I spent it in the service of my country. Today they seek to cover me with opprobrium and infamy. I am made the most unhappy of men: my liberty is taken from me, and I am separated from my aged father, my wife, and my children." - Toussaint L'Ouverture, memoirs written in a French prison, 1802. Context: L'Ouverture, a formerly enslaved man, led the revolution in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. After helping expel Spanish and British forces, he was seized by French troops in 1802 and deported to France, where he died in prison in 1803. Haiti declared independence in 1804.
questions.stem: Which of the following developments most directly inspired the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue to rise in revolt in 1791?
options: (A) The abolition of slavery in the British Empire.
(B) The wars of independence that freed the Spanish American republics from colonial rule.
(C) The French Revolution's ideals of liberty, which the enslaved claimed for themselves.
(D) The issuing of the Emancipation Proclamation in the United States.

questions.stimulus:
In August 1791, enslaved people across northern Saint-Domingue rose in a coordinated insurrection. Tradition holds that the revolt was planned at a vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman, led by the maroon leader Dutty Boukman — the beginning of the Haitian Revolution.

The uprising of August 1791 was meticulously planned: enslaved leaders coordinated across plantations, and on the night of August 14 a vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman — led by the maroon Dutty Boukman — sealed the conspiracy. Within weeks northern Saint-Domingue was in flames; within two years the French Republic, desperate for soldiers, abolished slavery; within thirteen, Haiti was independent. The ceremony at Bois Caïman is remembered as the night the largest slave revolt in history began.

questions.stimulus:
'To slacken the tempo would mean falling behind. And those who fall behind get beaten. But we do not want to be beaten. One feature of the history of old Russia was the continual beatings she suffered because of her backwardness. She was beaten by the Mongol khans, by the Turkish beys, by the Swedish feudal lords, by the Polish and Lithuanian gentry, by the British and French capitalists, by the Japanese barons. All beat her because of her backwardness: military backwardness, cultural backwardness, political backwardness, industrial backwardness, agricultural backwardness. They beat her because it was profitable and could be done with impunity. Such is the law of the exploiters: to beat the backward and the weak. It is the jungle law of capitalism. You are backward, you are weak, therefore you are wrong; hence you can be beaten and enslaved. You are mighty, therefore you are right; hence we must be wary of you. That is why we must no longer lag behind.'

Source: Joseph Stalin, speech to industrial managers, February 4, 1931

questions.stimulus: In 1960, the township of Sharpeville became a symbol of South Africa's racial order. Under the apartheid laws, every Black South African man was required to carry a passbook, a small document recording where he was permitted to live and work. To be found in a city without the proper stamp meant arrest. On March 21, thousands of Black protesters gathered outside the Sharpeville police station, deliberately leaving their passbooks at home in a planned act of defiance. The police opened fire on the unarmed crowd, killing sixty-nine people, most of them shot in the back as they fled. The government's response was not reform but repression: the African National Congress and its rivals were banned, and leaders such as Nelson Mandela were driven underground and then imprisoned. For the white minority that held all political power, the massacre confirmed the need for ever harsher control. For Black South Africans, it proved that peaceful protest alone would not end a system that denied them citizenship in their own country. Sharpeville drew the world's attention to apartheid and pushed the liberation movement toward armed resistance. Four years later, Mandela stood trial for his life at Rivonia, using the courtroom to indict apartheid before the world. Although the regime survived for three more decades, Sharpeville marked the moment when South Africa's racial order became an international scandal rather than a domestic arrangement.

(B) Guaranteeing equal wages for all workers in the mines

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt's 1958 remarks on human rights, delivered on the tenth anniversary of the Universal Declaration: Where do universal rights begin? In small places, close to home — places so small and so close that they cannot be seen on any maps of the world. Yet they are the world of the individual person: the neighborhood he lives in, the school or college he attends, the factory, farm, or office where he works. These are the places where every man, woman, and child seeks equal justice, equal opportunity, and equal dignity without discrimination. Unless these rights have meaning there, they have little meaning anywhere. Without concerted citizen action to uphold them close to home, we shall look in vain for progress in the larger world. The Declaration itself, adopted in 1948, opens by recalling that disregard for human rights produced barbarous acts that outraged the conscience of mankind, and proclaims a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations.

questions.stimulus: At the height of their power, the Mongol khans ruled a vast domain where peoples who had once been enemies lived side by side in relative peace, and nearly every religion was tolerated. The legal code first issued under Chinggis Khan regulated relations among these peoples and opened a new era of international contact. From Eastern Europe to southern China, merchants and travelers could cross the well-guarded Mongol territories without fearing for their lives or goods. The great belt of Mongol land, covering or linking most of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, served as a bridge between the civilizations of the Eastern Hemisphere. Caravans and embassies crossing Mongol lands carried new foods, inventions, and ideas from one civilized region to another, and from settled societies to the nomads who acted as go-betweens. Safe roads enriched merchants and built wealthy, cosmopolitan cities, while the movement of crops and technologies became a powerful engine of economic and social development.

section_1b.directions: Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (a, b, and c). You have 40 minutes for this section.

q1.attribution: —Historian's account of why industrialization began in Britain, c. 1750–1850
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE factor that favored British industrialization according to the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of Britain's advantage in cotton textile manufacturing.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between British industrialization and industrialization in Japan after 1868.

sample_answers.a: One factor was abundant coal located near navigable water, giving British manufacturers cheap energy and cheap transport together.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the empire: British control of trade supplied raw cotton from the Americas and India while colonial and global markets bought finished cloth, guaranteeing demand for ever-greater output.
sample_answers.c: Britain industrialized through private enterprise over many decades with minimal state direction, while Japan's Meiji government deliberately planned industrialization from above — building railways, hiring foreign experts, and founding state factories.

q1.stimulus: Historians point to a fortunate combination in Britain: abundant coal near navigable water, high wages that made labor-saving machines profitable, a patent system that rewarded inventors, and a global empire that supplied cotton and bought cloth. No single factor was decisive — China had coal and markets, India had cotton and skills — but in Britain all the pieces were in place at once, and the empire's markets gave manufacturers a reason to keep expanding output.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Smith makes about economic behavior.
parts.b: Explain ONE way Smith's ideas reflected the commercial changes of eighteenth-century Britain.
parts.c: Explain ONE way industrial economies after 1850 diverged from Smith's vision of free markets.

sample_answers.a: Smith claims that people provide goods and services not from kindness but from self-interest — the baker sells bread to earn a living, and that self-interest feeds everyone.
sample_answers.b: His ideas reflected a Britain where markets, wage labor, and commercial farming were already replacing feudal obligation; he was describing — and justifying — the market economy growing up around him.
sample_answers.c: After 1850, governments intervened far beyond anything Smith endorsed: factory safety laws, public education, central banks, and eventually welfare states — because unregulated markets produced slums, depressions, and labor revolts that laissez-faire could not fix.

q2.stimulus: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves not to their humanity but to their self-love.

q3.attribution: Photograph of the Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale, England (1779)
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the bridge shown in the image.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the bridge illustrates the technological changes of the Industrial Revolution.
parts.c: Explain ONE environmental consequence of the iron industry centered in places like Coalbrookdale.

sample_answers.a: The bridge is a graceful single arch made entirely of cast iron — a material never before used at such scale for construction.
sample_answers.b: It shows iron moving from a craft material to an industrial one: coke-smelted iron made the metal cheap enough to build bridges, then railways and machines, transforming construction and transport.
sample_answers.c: The coke-fired furnaces devoured coal and forests, filling the Severn gorge with smoke and slag — Coalbrookdale became one of the first landscapes visibly scarred by industrial pollution.

q3.stimulus: Photograph of the Iron Bridge over the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, England, completed in 1779 — the first major bridge built of cast iron, standing in the heart of Britain's early industrial region.

q1.attribution: —Historian's account of working-class responses to industrialization, c. 1800–1900
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE working-class response to industrialization described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the differences in workers' political strategies across countries.
parts.c: Explain ONE similarity between labor movements in industrial Britain and industrial Germany.

sample_answers.a: British workers built trade unions and eventually a Labour Party, pursuing reform through organization and, after gaining the vote, through parliament.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the political system: where states permitted unions and voting, as in Britain, workers used them; where states repressed all organization, as in Russia, workers turned to illegal strikes and revolutionary councils.
sample_answers.c: In both countries, workers combined economic organization — unions and strikes for wages and hours — with political organization — parties demanding the vote and protective legislation — the same two-track strategy adapted to different regimes.

q1.stimulus: Industrial workers answered the factory system in strikingly different ways. British workers built trade unions and a Labour Party, winning the vote and then using it. German workers built the world's largest socialist party under Bismarck's hostile empire. Russian workers, denied any legal outlet, turned to strikes and soviets that exploded in 1905 and 1917. The miseries were similar — long hours, dangerous machines, crowded slums — but the politics depended on what each state allowed.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto, 1848
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Marx and Engels make in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects conditions in industrial Europe in 1848.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of the Manifesto's prediction that workers would unite across national boundaries.

sample_answers.a: They claim that all history is the history of class struggle and call on the workers of all countries to unite in revolution.
sample_answers.b: Written amid the revolutions of 1848, the passage reflects a Europe of factory slums, food riots, and uprisings — Marx and Engels believed the working class was about to overthrow capitalism as the bourgeoisie had overthrown feudalism.
sample_answers.c: In practice, workers repeatedly chose nation over class: in 1914, socialist parties across Europe voted for war credits and workers marched off to kill each other, showing national identity was stronger than the international solidarity Marx predicted.

q2.stimulus: A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of communism. The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. The workers have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. Working men of all countries, unite!

q3.attribution: Lewis Hine, 'A little spinner in the Mollahan Mills, Newberry, S.C.', 1908
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE detail of the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE way photographs like Hine's were used by reformers.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between child labor in industrial Britain and child labor in the United States in the early 1900s.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows a small girl, dwarfed by the spinning machinery, tending bobbins in a dim mill — her size against the machines makes her youth unmistakable.
sample_answers.b: Reformers used Hine's photographs as evidence in campaigns for child-labor laws: images of real children in mills made abstract statistics visible and shamed legislators and consumers into action.
sample_answers.c: Britain had restricted child labor by national Factory Acts decades earlier, beginning in the 1830s–40s, while in the United States regulation was left to the states, so Southern mills like Mollahan still employed children legally in 1908.

q3.stimulus: Lewis Hine's photograph 'A little spinner in the Mollahan Mills, Newberry, S.C.' (1908): a young girl working as a spinner in an American cotton mill, standing amid the machinery.

q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE reform undertaken during the Self-Strengthening Movement.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the movement's failure to prevent defeat by Japan in 1895.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity between the Self-Strengthening Movement and the later Hundred Days' Reforms of 1898.

sample_answers.a: The movement built modern arsenals and shipyards, such as those at Jiangnan and Fuzhou, translating Western technical books and training Chinese engineers to make rifles, steamships, and telegraphs.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the refusal to reform institutions: the Qing adopted Western weapons but kept the Confucian examination system, Manchu privilege, and a corrupt court — so Japan, which reformed its army, schools, and government together, won decisively.
sample_answers.c: Both movements shared the goal of strengthening China through selective Western borrowing without abandoning the imperial Confucian order — the reformers of 1898, like those of the 1860s, wanted a stronger dynasty, not a revolution.

q1.stimulus: After defeat in the Opium Wars and the devastation of the Taiping Rebellion, Qing officials such as Li Hongzhang and Zeng Guofan launched the Self-Strengthening Movement: arsenals, shipyards, railways, and schools teaching Western science — while preserving Confucian values and the imperial system. The slogan was 'Chinese learning as the foundation, Western learning for practical use.' It produced real ships and guns, but when the test came in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95, Japan's deeper reforms crushed the Chinese fleet.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Feng Guifen, Chinese scholar-official, 'On the Adoption of Western Knowledge,' 1861
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE thing Feng Guifen says China should learn from Westerners.
parts.b: Explain ONE way Feng's argument reflects the crisis facing the Qing dynasty in 1861.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Feng Guifen's program and the program of Japan's Meiji reformers.

sample_answers.a: He says China should learn Western military technology — 'solid ships and effective guns' — and nothing else.
sample_answers.b: Written after China's defeats in the Opium Wars and during the Taiping Rebellion, the argument reflects desperation: the dynasty's survival required Western weapons, but Feng still could not imagine abandoning Confucian civilization itself.
sample_answers.c: Feng wanted to graft Western guns onto an unchanged Confucian state, while the Meiji reformers rebuilt Japan's institutions — abolishing the samurai class, creating conscript armies, and writing a constitution — transforming the state, not just its arsenal.

q2.stimulus: What we have to learn from the barbarians is only the one thing — solid ships and effective guns. If we learn their superior techniques and use them to defend ourselves, we can turn the tables on those who now threaten us.

q3.attribution: French political cartoon, 1898: 'China — the cake of kings... and of emperors'
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE detail of the cartoon.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the foreign scramble for concessions in China shown in the cartoon.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the cartoon illustrates the consequences of the Self-Strengthening Movement's failure.

sample_answers.a: The cartoon shows the rulers of Britain, Germany, Russia, France, and Japan literally slicing up a cake labeled China, dividing it among themselves while a Chinese mandarin looks on powerless.
sample_answers.b: One cause was China's evident military weakness after its 1895 defeat by Japan, which convinced each foreign power it had to seize ports, railways, and spheres of influence before rivals took them all.
sample_answers.c: The cartoon shows the price of half-reform: because Self-Strengthening never built a military or state strong enough to resist, China became an object to be divided — the very fate the movement had been launched to prevent.

q3.stimulus: French political cartoon from 1898 titled 'China — the cake of kings... and of emperors': Queen Victoria of Britain, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany, Tsar Nicholas II of Russia, Marianne of France, and the emperor of Japan carve up a cake labeled 'Chine' (China) while a Chinese official watches helplessly in the background.

section_2a.directions: Question 1 is based on the accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise. You are advised to spend 15 minutes reading and planning and 45 minutes writing your answer.

dbq.analysis_note: All pre-1900 excerpts are plain-language renderings of public-domain sources.

documents.source_line: Testimony of a child worker before the Sadler Committee, a parliamentary inquiry into factory conditions
documents.sourcing_note: A child witness speaking to members of Parliament; purpose of the inquiry is to expose conditions and build support for regulation. The child's plain account carries weight because it is firsthand, though selected by reformers.
documents.text_or_description: I began work at six in the morning and did not leave the mill until eight at night. When we grew tired the overlookers beat us with straps. I was eight years old, and my wages were a few pence a day.

documents.source_line: Report of a British factory inspector, appointed under the Factory Act
documents.sourcing_note: A government official reporting to the Home Office; purpose is to document violations of the new law. His medical language reflects the state's growing role in monitoring industrial life.
documents.text_or_description: I found children of ten and eleven working thirteen hours daily in heat, dust, and noise. Their growth is stunted, their limbs deformed, and their health broken before they reach adulthood. The law is evaded wherever no inspector watches.

documents.source_line: Samuel Smiles, Scottish writer, in Self-Help
documents.sourcing_note: A middle-class moralist writing for working-class readers; purpose is to preach self-improvement, not to describe workers' lives accurately. His optimism is itself evidence of a new ideology: that industrial society rewards individual effort.
documents.text_or_description: Heaven helps those who help themselves. The spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual. The poorest laborer may rise by industry, thrift, and perseverance, whatever his beginnings.

documents.source_line: Friedrich Engels, German observer, in The Condition of the Working Class in England
documents.sourcing_note: A German radical observing Manchester for a European audience; purpose is to indict industrial capitalism. His statistics impress, but his revolutionary conclusions shape what he chooses to show.
documents.text_or_description: The workers' districts are a chaos of narrow alleys, filth, and crumbling houses. Cholera and fever carry off hundreds each year, yet the mills grow richer and their owners build fine houses on the hills above the smoke.

documents.source_line: The People's Charter, petition of the Chartist movement to Parliament
documents.sourcing_note: A working-class movement addressing Parliament; purpose is to demand political rights. The petition shows workers responding to industrial conditions not with despair but with organized political action.
documents.text_or_description: We, the working men of Britain, demand a vote for every man, secret ballots, and an end to property qualifications for Parliament. We who create the wealth of the nation are denied any voice in the laws that govern us.

documents.license: Public domain (1835 engraving by T. Allom/J. Tingle, from Baines’s History of the Cotton Manufacture)
documents.source_line: Engraving of power-loom weaving in a British cotton mill, 1835
documents.sourcing_note: A contemporary illustration for a history of the cotton industry; purpose is to show the new technology. The image captures the transformed workplace: rows of machines tended by workers, mostly women and children, under one roof.
documents.text_or_description: The engraving shows a large mill room filled with power looms, each tended by a worker. Shafts and belts overhead drive dozens of machines at once, and the workers move among them in a crowded, regimented space.

documents.source_line: Original chart: approximate population of Manchester, 1750-1851 (created for this assessment; no external URL)
documents.sourcing_note: A modern compilation of commonly cited census estimates for this assessment; purpose is to show the scale of urbanization. Explosive city growth is the demographic face of industrial transformation.
documents.text_or_description: Manchester's population grew from about 25,000 in 1750 to about 75,000 in 1801, about 142,000 in 1831, and about 303,000 in 1851 — a twelvefold increase in a century, driven by migration from the countryside to the mills.

dbq.prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the extent to which industrialization transformed the lives of workers in Britain in the period c. 1750-1900.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: argue transformation was profound (new workplace, new cities, new politics) while noting continuities (poverty, long hours, and inequality predated factories; Doc 3's self-help ideology shows some workers embraced the new order); corroborate harsh conditions across Docs 1, 2, and 4; qualify by distinguishing factory workers from other laborers; Docs 5 and 7 together show a new urban working class becoming a political force.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (audience/purpose: a child testifying to reform-minded MPs); Doc 2 (context: an inspector enforcing a new law); Doc 3 (purpose: a moralist preaching to workers, revealing middle-class ideology); Doc 4 (point of view: a revolutionary using Manchester as evidence); Doc 5 (audience: Parliament, from the workers themselves).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate British industrialization within the Agricultural Revolution displacing rural labor, the Napoleonic Wars' economic disruption, the Reform era's political ferment, and Britain's position as the first industrial nation whose experience others would follow.

evidence.describe: All seven describable; strongest: Docs 1, 2, 4 (conditions), Docs 6, 7 (the new industrial world), Doc 5 (workers' response).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the Factory Acts (1833, 1844, 1847 Ten Hours Act); the Mines Act (1842); the growth of trade unions and the TUC (1868); the Second Reform Act (1867) extending the vote; public health reforms after cholera epidemics; Luddite machine-breaking (1811-1816).
evidence.support: 'Transformed' line: Docs 1, 2, 4, 6, 7. 'Continuities/limits' line: Docs 3 (ideology of individual effort), Doc 5 (workers still voteless, still organizing as before). Doc 5 cuts both ways: new political agency within unchanged exclusion.

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'extent' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

dbq.sample_thesis: Industrialization transformed workers' lives to a great extent by moving labor from countryside to city, from home to factory, and from resignation to organized political action; yet the transformation was incomplete, because poverty, exhausting hours, and political exclusion persisted, and workers themselves had to force every reform through decades of struggle.
dbq.title: Industrialization and British Workers

section_2b.directions: Answer the question below. You have 40 minutes.

leq.exam: AP World History: Modern, May 2027 (Fall 2026 CED) - single required prompt, 40 min, 15% of score
leq.process_note: New-format LEQ: the student chooses their own reasoning process and evidence. The target process above is a coverage tag for bank balance, not a constraint on the student.
leq.prompt: In the period c. 1750-c. 1900, Great Britain industrialized early while other states industrialized later, often more rapidly and under different conditions. Develop an argument that compares the processes and social consequences of industrialization in Great Britain and in one other industrializing state in this period. Your response may focus on any example(s) that support your argument. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

rubric_map.thesis_1: Presents a historically defensible thesis that responds to the prompt and establishes a line of reasoning.
rubric_map.contextualization_1: Describes a broader historical context relevant to the prompt. Acceptable context: the global spread of industrial technology, competition among states, different resource endowments, or the social disruptions of urbanization.
rubric_map.evidence_examples_1: Identifies at least two specific historical examples relevant to the argument. Acceptable examples: Britain's textile mills and coal/steam base vs. Japan's state-led Meiji industrialization, Germany's tariff-protected heavy industry, Russia's railway-driven industrialization under Witte, or the United States' continental scale.
rubric_map.evidence_supports_argument_1: Uses the examples to support the argument rather than merely listing or describing them. Examples must support explicit comparisons of processes (how industrialization happened) and consequences (urbanization, labor conditions, class formation) in both states.
rubric_map.analysis_reasoning_1: Uses the targeted historical reasoning process to structure the argument. Comparison: identifies similarities and differences in both process and consequences, and explains them (e.g., timing, state role, resources).
rubric_map.analysis_complex_understanding_1: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the historical development: e.g., qualifies the argument by explaining nuance or contradiction, evaluates multiple perspectives, or connects the argument across themes or time periods.

leq.sample_thesis: Britain's gradual, market-driven industrialization and Japan's rapid, state-directed industrialization produced similar social consequences - crowded cities, harsh factory labor, and new working classes - but differed fundamentally in process: Britain industrialized from commercial advantage over generations, while Japan compressed the transformation into decades through deliberate state policy.
leq.evidence_directions: Strong responses compare the same dimensions in both cases (e.g., role of the state, pace, labor conditions) rather than narrating one country then the other. Common pairings: Britain-Japan, Britain-Germany, Britain-Russia, Britain-United States.
